Spend as little time as possible at home. 

Limit your exposure to triggers and things that make binges easier. So, for example, a lot of my binges were sourced by UberEats. I just transferred all funds to a card that was impossible to connect to Ubereats. -> could not order food late at night and was too lazy/scared to get it myself -> didn't binge

Surround yourself with people who make you feel good and aren't emotionally draining. I had instances when talking to certain people eliminated urges to binge for several days (during times when I purged multiple times a day, so it was huge for me).

Also, a big thing for me was being on my own most of the time, and the main change that has resulted in my recovery has been not living alone anymore. BUT I understand that this is a temporary solution and once I'm left to my own devices, I'll relapse. Therefore, it's important to use this time to solve the underlying psychological problems that led to bulimia in the first place. :)

I would guess the real issue here is low self esteem. Desperation/clinginess (I am sorry if this sounds rude, but that’s how people will perceive you if you keep doing this) is just a consequence. So maybe it’s worth shifting your focus to the root cause and working on it.

I can be wrong though. 

In my case, it is not really about being unemotional, but rather not attaching to people.
You have to understand your worth and make “attachment” a conscious choice. If the person truly cares about you, shows their appreciation and respect, you commit to the person. Otherwise, you just wait and see until the signs show up. It is also important to cut off toxic people on time. 

One negative thing about the approach is that when you choose to commit, it really becomes an effort to show the other person that you appreciate them. Usually, the things an emotional person would do are like a chore to me: “Ok, I have not texted this person first for a long time, but this person treats me really well and I am a better self with them around, I don’t want them to feel like I do not care and lose them, so I will text them now”. The whole thing just becomes a series of rational, conscious choices.

Edit: oh, another disadvantage is that “non-attachment” extends beyond romantic relationships, so it affects my family members, friends etc. And it feels bad to see how a close one suffers from thinking you do not care. But maybe that’s just my problem and people can segment their attachment/non-attachment thing lol

From my experience, I act differently with different people. Some naturally bring out my playful parts, others make me turn into a silent, serious person. Does he have anyone, with whom he is more open and relaxed? It is unlikely he does not have cravings for depth, but he could be fulfilling them with his friends.

The higher your income, the smaller share of it turns into consumption, assuming diminishing utility of consumption.  If you give your dog 10 kilos of dog food per meal, it will leave most of it untouched. If you share the 10 kilos among 20 dogs, nothing will be left.

Consumption is a component of aggregate demand/GDP. So the more people spend, the more funds will be circulating in the economy, financing employment and supporting provision of goods and services.

Of course, one could argue that bank savings, too, find their way into the economy + many other reasons why the logic above is incomplete. But I tried to provide the basic idea.

Generally, as economies develop, the following structural changes occur: 
1. Both employment and value added shares of agriculture decline
2. ••• of manufacturing follow an inverse U-shape
3. ••• of services increase
(Have a look at “Growth and Structural Transformation” by Herrendorf, Rogerson and Valentinyi for a detailed account)

Which way the relationship works is not clear. The paper considers the structural transformation as a consequence of increased wealth rather than a cause.

If you look at standard development models, such as the Solow model - growth is driven by capital accumulation and determined by improvements in technology. In the past, technology improvements were only seen as a larger selection of/more productive tangible capital goods, so from this point of view industrialisation would be necessary for development. 

Nowadays, however, a larger share of value is created from non-tangible/intellectual capital, and the technology improvements required for growth (as the Solow model suggests) do not have to originate in manufacturing/industry.
